1.tense: Right now you are holding this without forcing it toward an answer.
1.verb: bearing what must be borne without breaking or hardening
1.place: at the seed's edge, before anything has been chosen
1.ask: Next time someone you love is in something hard, stay in it with them and don't solve it. Ten minutes beside them is plenty.
1.core:
You can carry weight and keep it from pressing down on anything else. A thing is still undecided, and you don't shove it into a shape to feel better — you keep standing there, and that turns out to be what holding looks like when it works. Under something unformed, you stay put, and staying doesn't take your footing from under you. Whoever is nearby picks that up. Some of them soften because of it.

There is something new in your life that has not declared itself. Stay with it the way you would sit with a person in a hard week: no fixing, no deciding what it is. Give it attention for seven days and keep the question open. You may feel a pull to call it by a name before it is ready. Notice the pull. Nothing has to follow from noticing.
1.sheetLine: You can carry what's unformed without forcing it into shape.

2.tense: Soon a future you cannot see will arrive and you are already bracing for it.
2.verb: bearing what must be borne without breaking or hardening
2.place: at the seed's edge, before anything has been chosen
2.ask: This week, answer the help or invitation you left sitting and give one thing back in return. Then stop counting.
2.core:
You are gripping some untried thing hard enough that it cannot move. You are bracing for a load before it has arrived, and what was strength sets into something the thing itself can feel. It's striking how much pressure you can put on something that isn't heavy yet. Nothing about next year gets clearer from a tighter grip; it just gets smaller. The grip is doing work, but not the work you want.

Something was offered to you and left untouched. Take it this week — the help, the invitation, the hand held out — and give one thing back in return, without a tally. One exchange gets the current moving both ways. You do not have to settle the whole future to make it.
2.sheetLine: Bracing for a weight that hasn't arrived is its own weight.

3.tense: You once stood at a door carrying something and set it down before you went through.
3.verb: bearing what must be borne without breaking or hardening
3.place: at the seed's edge, before anything has been chosen
3.ask: The duty that already ended is still on you. Put it down this afternoon — somewhere real, a drawer or a shelf — and don't pick it back up before evening.
3.core:
Holding has stopped being something you do. A new thing is nearby and it hasn't been picked up at all — not because it isn't worth it, but because reaching for it now looks like the last reach did. The seed is there. You haven't put it in ground. That happens after a weight lands wrong, and it doesn't mean the ability is gone. It means the last one sat heavy and you stopped reaching for the next.

Start smaller. Some duty you finished still has your arms full — a responsibility held past its finish, something that now holds you back more than it holds anything up. Set it somewhere real this afternoon and go through to evening without picking it back up.
3.sheetLine: Nothing has been picked up since the last thing weighed too much.

4.tense: The door you are holding open was opened by your own hand, and you don't remember it.
4.verb: bearing what must be borne without breaking or hardening
4.place: at the seed's edge, before anything has been chosen
4.ask: Ask yourself which thing you'd hate most to lose and haven't yet picked. Then take one step toward it this week — a footfall, no more.
4.core:
You are bearing more than you notice, and standing under it keeps several things upright. You would probably call it luck, or circumstance, or not your doing. You have kept them steady a while and not put your own name on the steadying. Somebody who relies on it can feel that it holds, even when you can't tell. That is the part that stays out of sight.

There is something you might actually want, and you have not let yourself want it plainly. Pick that out — not the reasonable choice, the one you would hate to lose — and take one step the size of a footfall toward it this week. No plan past that step. Face it and move.
4.sheetLine: You are holding things up and not counting your hands.

1.tense: You are holding what you chose to hold, and it is holding well.
1.verb: bearing what must be borne without going rigid
1.place: where you decide what this, not that, means — the line of your own going, chosen and held
1.ask: Next time someone's in the middle of something hard, don't reach for the fix. Stay beside them, and if they ask what you notice about them, say it plainly and stop there.
1.core:
There's a steadiness in you that doesn't need to be tested to be trusted. Somewhere close to home, you've picked up something that asks a lot, and you carry it while staying aimed at what you chose — no crushing, no bracing, just weight meeting a steady grip.

The next turn of the same steadiness is being beside someone in trouble without taking their load onto your own back. Not fixing. Staying in contact, keeping your own side, and letting them hear what you notice about them only if they ask. That's connection that holds without merging — your grip stays yours. The same steadiness that carries the weight also knows how to keep its hands off someone else's.

ring true
1.sheetLine: You hold what you chose without gripping it to death.

2.tense: You are already bracing against a weight that has not yet been set down in front of you.
2.verb: bearing what must be borne without going rigid
2.place: where you decide what this, not that, means — the line of your own going, chosen and held
2.ask: Over one week, note what you took on and what someone else did. Shift one piece of the split so it's even, then stop counting for the rest of the week.
2.core:
You can hold what has to be held. That's real. And at the far edge of it, the grip is closed on things that no longer need holding — a fixed plan, an outcome you already chose, a weight you're bracing on someone else's behalf. What was resilient strength has started to read as rigidity.

Getting back to even isn't more effort. It's looking at what you're actually carrying, naming what each piece costs, and putting one of them back in someone else's hands — then stopping. Not punishment, not scorekeeping. Just proportion. The strength is still yours; it just needs a target you actually chose, not one you gripped ahead of time. You'll know it's working when the week stops feeling like a thing you survive.

The cell must be specific about the re-share and the stop, in the same week, small enough to be seen.
2.sheetLine: Bracing for weight that isn't here yet is its own weight.

3.tense: You have been waiting at a door that closed a long time ago.
3.verb: bearing what must be borne without going rigid
3.place: where you decide what this, not that, means — the line of your own going, chosen and held
3.ask: Pick something you're still carrying out of duty or protest, set it down on purpose — not lost, not thrown — and let your hands rest open for a short while.
3.core:
Holding has stopped feeling possible. Where you once carried things without breaking, now the pressure lands and something in you lets go instead of standing. This isn't weakness — it's a body that learned holding is dangerous, and it moved to protect you. The direction you had is behind you, and you're still at that door.

What pulls you forward isn't more grip. It's clearing. Something no longer serves you and you're carrying it out of habit, so set it down deliberately. Not thrown away in panic — laid down. One deliberate release, and a stretch where your hands aren't full. That stretch is where direction comes back.

The ask must not push effort or feeling into the starved place — it pulls from the release, which is the inner motion already running.
3.sheetLine: You can set something down without dropping everything.

4.tense: The direction you are steering by has been set without you noticing that you set it.
4.verb: bearing what must be borne without going rigid
4.place: where you decide what this, not that, means — the line of your own going, chosen and held
4.ask: Of everything you're steering toward, name the one whose loss would sting most — to yourself, plainly, no plan — and turn toward it once today.
4.core:
There is a strength here you don't count as yours. You hold things under pressure — a job, a person, a promise — and it doesn't register as anything, only as what was required. The same with letting go: sometimes it was strength, and you filed it under 'I got lucky' or 'it was fine anyway.'

Nothing to prove. Just take the wheel back into your own hands in one place. Look at what you're already pointed at, and name the one whose loss would sting most. Let yourself want it, plainly, to yourself — no plan, no announcement. Then turn toward it once. What you actually chose is what's already been holding you up.

The ask must be a single turn, not a plan, and must not overrule the person's own account of what they've been doing.
4.sheetLine: The direction you're steering by is one you chose.

1.tense: You are holding this steady right now, and it is not costing you a thing.
1.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
1.place: the place where weight and attention land before any reasoning has arrived
1.ask: When someone close to you is sitting in something heavy, let it reach you before you do anything about it — stay in contact a while, no fixing, no lifting.
1.core:
You can tell what needs your weight and what doesn't, and you do it without straining. A friend comes to you in trouble and you hold it steady; you don't go hard, you don't lecture, you don't turn their mess into your worry. That's what bearing something well looks like — the shape stays, nothing snaps, nothing turns to stone.

What this balance is free to feed next is being reached. Most people holding a hard thing are already bracing before it lands; you have the calm to let it land. So when someone close to you is sitting in something heavy, let it reach you before you do anything about it. Stay in contact a while, and don't fix or lift it. There's a version of held where you stay soft, and this is the week to find it.
1.sheetLine: You can hold what's heavy and stay human while you do it.

2.tense: You will have braced for something that hasn't happened yet, and the bracing is the hurt.
2.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
2.place: the place where weight and attention land before any reasoning has arrived
2.ask: Find a place where you're holding tighter than the situation asks. Put it in fair proportion — enough and no more — and when it's right, quit.
2.core:
The grip is running ahead of you. Somewhere past the next bend a thing might go wrong, and your body already has its hands around it — holding the friend upright before they've stumbled, holding the plan before the week has spoken, holding a door shut on something that may not come. What used to be strength is setting like concrete. The tighter you hold, the less you hear what's actually there, and the people you're holding upright can feel the squeeze.

Restoring proportion is the work. Locate one place where you're holding tighter than the situation asks. Put it in fair proportion — enough and no more — then quit while it's right. You've been hauling weight for ground nobody has stood on yet, and setting it down is how the hands remember they're hands.
2.sheetLine: You're gripping next week before it has arrived.

3.tense: You were holding so much pressure for so long that putting anything down felt like it would finally finish you.
3.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
3.place: the place where weight and attention land before any reasoning has arrived
3.ask: Take something you've kept a grip on and set it down deliberately — not a slip, a choice — then leave your hands open a day or two.
3.core:
When the pressure came, holding wasn't safe anymore — you couldn't take the extra weight and you didn't let anyone see that, so what happened is you stopped taking weight at all. Something goes wrong now and the hands don't reach. You stand near the door, past the moment, telling yourself there's nothing you can add. The strength hasn't gone; the grip went, and behind the not-reaching there's a decision already made that whatever you hold will get crushed or taken.

Release skipped its proper place — it moved in before the job was finished. Take something you've kept a grip on. Set it down deliberately, not by losing it, and leave your hands empty for a day or two. Ending a hold on purpose is not the same as having nothing to hold, and the body learns the difference only by doing it.
3.sheetLine: You stopped reaching, not because you can't hold, but because holding stopped feeling safe.

4.tense: You are already the steady presence in the room, and when someone says so you credit the situation rather than the hands.
4.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
4.place: the place where weight and attention land before any reasoning has arrived
4.ask: Think of something you used to move toward before the steadying began — a craft, a place, a person — and face it again plainly, for its own sake.
4.core:
There's holding happening in your life that you'd put on the situation rather than on yourself. Someone falls apart and you keep your feet; you'd say anyone would. The room holds because you keep holding it, and that you can is not something you claim. What's harder to see is the second thing riding along: the aim. Strength needs somewhere to point, and yours is still pointed where it was before you learned to brace — which is why nothing arranged feels finished.

The part of you that knew where to face came before you got good at carrying. Think of something you used to move toward before the steadying took over — a craft, a town, a person, a stretch of work you actually wanted. Face it again plainly, not as a duty. That pull is yours; it was there before the shoulders were.
4.sheetLine: You steady the room and call it nothing. The aiming is also you.

1.tense: You are carrying the weight now, and it is staying workable in your hands.
1.verb: bearing what has to be held without going rigid around it
1.place: the care that lets something grow at its own pace
1.ask: Next time someone close is struggling, sit with it a few minutes — and keep your own feet, your own view, your own evening. Not merging, not fixing. Alongside.
1.core:
You can carry a lot without going hard about it. When something you're tending is under strain, you don't clamp down and you don't drop it — you bear what's there, which is why what's around you grows without being rushed or squeezed. That's the rare part, and it's in your hands today.

Where this can still grow is at the edge of the people you're tending. When someone close is carrying something heavy, there's a pull to take all of it onto yourself. Feel what they're carrying with them instead — and keep your own side of it. Their strain doesn't have to become yours to be honoured. For now, that's the practice: closeness that doesn't dissolve the line between you.
1.sheetLine: You hold what's heavy, and it stays workable in your hands.

2.tense: You are already bracing for a version of events that has not arrived yet.
2.verb: bearing what has to be held without going rigid around it
2.place: the care that lets something grow at its own pace
2.ask: When you're carrying more than your share for someone, adjust it once — hand a piece back, or take something you've been going without — then stop counting and carry only what's yours.
2.core:
Your strength is working too hard ahead of schedule. Nothing has gone wrong yet and you're already steadying everything that might, carrying weight nobody put on you, standing in for people who could stand themselves. What you're doing is care. It has gone past what the moment asks for.

Fairness loosens it, and fairness is a small correction, not a verdict. Somewhere in what you're carrying there's a share that isn't yours — something you took on for someone who could hold it, or something you're doing that no one asked for. Set that piece down, and it can go back to whoever it belongs to. Or take something you've been going without. Then stop counting. The load evens out and what you carry goes back to the size of the day.
2.sheetLine: You're bracing for trouble that hasn't arrived yet.

3.tense: You stood at a door holding everything, and it felt too dangerous to keep holding.
3.verb: bearing what has to be held without going rigid around it
3.place: the care that lets something grow at its own pace
3.ask: Take a worry, an outcome, a grip you can't open — set it down on purpose for a day. Not forever. Just set it down and notice your hands empty.
3.core:
Holding anything feels risky now, so it stopped. When pressure came, whatever you were carrying set itself down without asking you — and the care you have for growing things went quiet with it. You're still here. This part of you didn't leave; it just isn't being trusted right now.

Gripping harder isn't what restores it. The other direction is: putting something down on purpose, the way you'd close a book at the end of a chapter rather than dropping it. Choose a worry, an outcome you can't steer, a decision you keep carrying — set it down deliberately. Not because you failed. Because it's finished with you. Empty hands for a day, and see what they feel like when something new comes to be held.
3.sheetLine: You stood at the door with everything, and set it down.

4.tense: You have been carrying a load for a long while and calling it nothing in particular.
4.verb: bearing what has to be held without going rigid around it
4.place: the care that lets something grow at its own pace
4.ask: Think of something you've been growing — a person, a project, a habit — and put into words what first drew you to it. Then look at it plainly, as it is now.
4.core:
There's strength in how you hold things, and you don't count it as anything. What you've been tending — people, work, a life — has kept going under pressure, and your account of it is that you were just there. You've been carrying a lot and calling it circumstance.

The pull that started it is smaller and older than the load. Before all this, something drew you toward what you're now holding — you chose it, wanted it, saw it as worth tending. That pull is still the honest name for what's happening. Go back to it. Look at what you've been growing and let yourself see it as something you chose and still choose, not just a weight that landed on you. What you're holding has your fingerprints on it.
4.sheetLine: You carry a great deal and call it nothing in particular.

1.tense: Right now you can take the pressure and still reach toward the person beside you.
1.verb: to bear the weight and keep the shape that carries it
1.place: where the plan gets made and the structure has to hold
1.ask: Ask someone close what these days have been like for them. Listen past the first answer — the second sentence usually holds the true one. Don't fix anything. Stay in it as long as they'll let you.
1.core:
You can hold a lot and still be near whoever is carrying something. That isn't small — most people either go hard and lose the person, or go soft and lose the structure. You do both at once, and the people you organize stay people to you.

Put that toward someone instead of a task. Ask one person close to you what these days have actually been like, then don't move to fix it. Listen until they say the real thing, usually the second or third sentence, and take it in without armor. You give up no hold by doing it. The other side of holding that carrying alone can't give you is this — you're in it with them, not above it.
1.sheetLine: You can hold the weight and stay near the person carrying theirs.

2.tense: You'll be gripping the shape of what's coming long before anyone asks you to.
2.verb: to bear the weight and keep the shape that carries it
2.place: where the plan gets made and the structure has to hold
2.ask: You're carrying something nobody handed you. Tell whoever it touches, ask if it's actually yours, and act on their answer — even if that means setting it down.
2.core:
Where you set the pattern, the grip has gone past what the job needs. You're bracing for a future nobody's written yet — pre-deciding, holding the frame so tightly it can't flex. Under strain, strength like yours starts to read as rigid to the people inside it. The structure holds. The room inside it doesn't.

Loosen a hold. Tell whoever it touches that you've been carrying something no one gave you, and ask if it's yours. Then do what they say, even if the answer is put it down. That isn't giving up the reins — it's letting the exchange run both ways like it used to. The pattern stays. You stop being the only one holding it up, which is the point.
2.sheetLine: You're bracing for a future nobody's written yet.

3.tense: The pressure came and you stepped back from the frame you used to stand in.
3.verb: to bear the weight and keep the shape that carries it
3.place: where the plan gets made and the structure has to hold
3.ask: Do the smallest piece of something you've let go slack — one call, one list, an hour — and leave the result exactly as it lands. No shaping after.
3.core:
Holding got hard the last time it mattered, and you stepped out of the pattern rather than stay in it. You can see what needs organizing. You watch from the side now, and the watching has its own strain. Standing at a door that closed behind you.

You don't have to want the outcome to do the next small act. Take something you let go slack, do the smallest piece of it today, then leave the result alone — no shaping it after. That's the release you've been waiting to feel ready for. It doesn't arrive as a feeling; it arrives as the act you did anyway, hands open after.
3.sheetLine: You're standing in a doorway that already closed behind you.

4.tense: You are keeping the structure standing and calling it nothing worth noticing.
4.verb: to bear the weight and keep the shape that carries it
4.place: where the plan gets made and the structure has to hold
4.ask: Think back to what first made you want to build things that hold, and face it again this week — just turn toward it, nothing more.
4.core:
The building happens and you file it under just handling it. Structures hold around you and people lean, while something in you waits for permission to want any of it. The strength is real. You haven't put your name on it.

Go back to why you started. Something drew you toward making things hold together, long before it became work, and it's still findable if you look. Face that again this week — just turn toward it, nothing more. Wanting it plainly, no apology attached, is the earlier form of what you're doing. Radiance grows from that, not from another year of not noticing.
4.sheetLine: You keep it standing and call it nothing worth naming.

1.tense: You are holding what was handed to you, and the form is steady in your arms.
1.verb: bearing what is handed down, holding a form steady while it passes to the next
1.place: the shared ground where meaning is kept and handed forward
1.ask: Choose a custom or story your people keep, and stay with it through the next stretch when it feels hollow. Keep it going. Don't repair what's thin in it yet.
1.core:
You can carry what your people hand down without gripping it so hard it cracks. The form stays; the warmth inside it stays. That's not hardness — it's a load that knows how to give at the edges. The ritual you keep still leaves space for whoever is standing nearby, and they can feel that, not just follow it.

Your strength here is built to be shared, not decided alone. So let someone reach you in it. Choose one of the sayings or observances you keep — a meal, a phrase, a way of marking a day — and stay in contact with it through a hard stretch instead of setting it down or forcing it back to life. Let it be touched by what you and the others are carrying now. What holds will show itself without your hand closing on it.
1.sheetLine: You hold the form steady and still let it move.

2.tense: Soon you will be gripping the old forms hard enough that nothing new can enter them.
2.verb: bearing what is handed down, holding a form steady while it passes to the next
2.place: the shared ground where meaning is kept and handed forward
2.ask: Look at how your shared life is arranged — who does what, who carries which part — and adjust the share once so it's fair. Then stop tuning. Leave the rest alone.
2.core:
You can feel yourself bracing ahead, holding the line on how things have been done. The grip is strong, and from the outside it looks like the custom itself stiffening, not you. What was resilience starts to look like rigidity, and the people who love the thing you're protecting start to drift from it.

That grip isn't wrong, it's just out of proportion. Something in how your shared life is arranged has gone lopsided, and the fix isn't tighter holding. Look at one arrangement — who does what, who carries which part — and adjust the share once so it's fair between the people involved. Just that. Then stop. Holding the old shape past the point where it fits serves the shape, not the people.
2.sheetLine: What you grip to save, you're squeezing out of shape.

3.tense: You set the load down a while back, and you have been standing in the draft since.
3.verb: bearing what is handed down, holding a form steady while it passes to the next
3.place: the shared ground where meaning is kept and handed forward
3.ask: Stop doing one customary thing — a greeting, a small observance, a phrase — for a week, on purpose. Notice the space it leaves. Then decide whether it comes back.
3.core:
You used to carry what your people handed down, and somewhere you handed it off. Not to anyone else — you just stopped holding it. The meals, the phrases that used to come without thinking. You're upright, but the load isn't across your shoulders, and behind it there's a door you haven't looked at in a while.

What's meant to come next isn't carrying it harder. Something has finished, and your hands know it. Stop doing one customary thing — a greeting, a small family observance — for a week, deliberately. Just that. Leave the space where it was, and see whether it asks to come back or whether the room is lighter without it. Either answer is a place to stand.
3.sheetLine: You stopped carrying it and said nothing about it.

4.tense: You keep the old forms going, and you have not once called it strength.
4.verb: bearing what is handed down, holding a form steady while it passes to the next
4.place: the shared ground where meaning is kept and handed forward
4.ask: Think of a tradition someone first showed you. Sit with the memory of them doing it, and feel again the pull that first made you pick it up.
4.core:
Ask about the words you remember, the date you keep, how the thing is done, and you'll say you just do it, or that it's not a big deal, or that somebody else really holds it. Keeping it going has kept happening, and has kept happening a long time. You're just the last person you credit for it.

There's a draw underneath this that you didn't call a draw. Something in it caught you early — a person, a way of doing it, a moment you wouldn't want to lose. Go back to that. Think of a tradition someone first showed you, sit with the memory of them doing it, and feel again the pull that first made you pick it up. Knowing what you're steering by is half of knowing you've been steering at all.
4.sheetLine: You've been keeping it alive and calling it nothing.

1.tense: Right now you are holding what needs holding without squeezing it shut.
1.verb: Bearing what has to be held.
1.place: In the room where you feel what others feel, alongside them.
1.ask: Next time someone close is in something hard, stay there with them a few minutes and offer nothing that fixes it — no advice, no bright side.
1.core:
You're in a stretch where you can stand beside someone in something hard and not require it to move. You feel what they're carrying without either of you vanishing into the other. Not many people can do that quietly, and the ones close to you can feel when you're doing it.

One more thing this balance is free to feed: staying near while it stays hard. Sit with them, bring nothing that solves it, and don't rush to fill the quiet. That doesn't load them up, and it doesn't take you under either. What the two of you find in that time isn't something either of you could have made alone.
1.sheetLine: You can hold someone without crushing them or being crushed.

2.tense: You're gripping the thing before the moment gets here.
2.verb: Bearing what has to be held.
2.place: In the room where you feel what others feel, alongside them.
2.ask: Where you carry the whole load for someone, give back a piece that's theirs and let a piece of yours be carried by them.
2.core:
When it's going well, you stand beside someone and let what they feel move through you without either of you disappearing. That's still in you. But lately you're bracing for what hasn't arrived. What was steady bearing has turned into carrying everything — every tension around you — so the next hard feeling finds you already tight. It's harder to sit with anyone while your hands are full. Keep going this way and you'll do the one thing that would hurt: stop letting anyone reach you.

Let the weight move both directions. Give back something you've been carrying for someone else, then say something you're carrying to whoever can take it. One in, one out, nothing settled. A balance you keep calculating stops being flow.
2.sheetLine: Holding everything makes it harder to feel what you're holding.

3.tense: The place where you feel what others feel is still waiting at a door that closed already.
3.verb: Bearing what has to be held.
3.place: In the room where you feel what others feel, alongside them.
3.ask: Set down the weight you still carry for someone who no longer needs it, and leave an afternoon this week unclaimed.
3.core:
The flatness you're in has a shape: an old defense still up, and the room where this strength lives still waiting at a boundary that moved on. You hold from behind a shield now. When the moment comes to be with someone in what they're feeling, hands that are too full can't reach.

Releasing works where pushing doesn't. Set a held weight down — a routine kept out of habit, a burden that belongs to someone else now — and leave an afternoon empty. Nothing gets handed over, nothing gets accomplished. Empty hands are the first thing that makes contact possible again.
3.sheetLine: Put down what you still carry, then let your hands be empty.

4.tense: You're holding people up right now, and you'd say it was just the circumstances.
4.verb: Bearing what has to be held.
4.place: In the room where you feel what others feel, alongside them.
4.ask: Spend an hour this week moving toward something you want that has nothing to do with what anyone needs from you.
4.core:
You have been the steady one for people going through it — the one who could stand in the middle of the mess and not break. You call that being around. That isn't something in the air; it's your strength, being used. Nobody asked you to name it, so you haven't.

Before you were carrying them, you had a pull of your own — something you wanted for yourself. Get near it again, an hour or so, long enough to remember the feel of it. This isn't a duty. It's the thing that was drawing you before anyone needed you to hold them up.
4.sheetLine: What they lean on is yours. Take an hour back.

1.tense: A load is being carried well here, and nothing in the hands is clenched around it.
1.verb: bearing what has weight, without turning rigid under it
1.place: on the road toward a goal, where the going is steady and long
1.ask: Ask somebody on the same road how they're bearing it — no fix coming, just sit with them in it for a while.
1.core:
You're carrying weight on the way to something, and the way you're doing it is the right way: steady, unforced, the load held rather than crushed. Nothing is being bent to fit your grip. There's room beside you for what other people are carrying. A good version of this looks like holding what's yours and not reaching into what isn't.

The one crack is your own: when the pace picks up, the hands tighten first. So put a small appointment in the week for somebody on the same road, and sit with them in what's heavy for them without solving any of it. It's an invitation, not a duty. What they say, you leave theirs. What you notice, you keep as yours. Then the road stays shared, and the load stays yours to hold.
1.sheetLine: You hold the load without crushing it.

2.tense: The pace is already being braced for a road that hasn't happened yet, and the bracing is winning.
2.verb: bearing what has weight, without turning rigid under it
2.place: on the road toward a goal, where the going is steady and long
2.ask: Return something you've been holding past its place — a debt, a favor, a share you picked up — this week, then stop counting.
2.core:
Somewhere ahead on this road, something is being braced for so hard that your grip has stopped being strength. Every mile gets held like a worse one is coming. The extra grip feels like discipline from where you're standing, but the people moving beside you are feeling a hand that won't loosen. Nobody is asking you to bear any of this harder than you already are.

So make something even. Give back a debt, a favor, someone else's share you picked up and didn't put down — one exchange, this week, and then stop counting. A fair road takes one trade at a time and doesn't require you to know every mile before it arrives. The weight you put down isn't lost; it's put where it belongs.
2.sheetLine: You're gripping a road that hasn't arrived.

3.tense: Pressure landed, and the hands have stayed off the load since.
3.verb: bearing what has weight, without turning rigid under it
3.place: on the road toward a goal, where the going is steady and long
3.ask: Give one afternoon to nothing you'd count as productive — a walk with no destination, no outcome produced.
3.core:
There's a road you were on, and you're at the side of it, holding nothing. That isn't a failure of strength; at some point the next weight looked like it would break, so the hands came off. The goal hasn't moved. Only the grip did. You may not be able to say when that happened, and you don't have to.

What's needed first is not more strain into a body that's already spent. Put the whole load down — not just today's part — and leave your hands empty a while. An afternoon, a walk, no outcome to produce. When nothing is being carried, the room to stand there at all shows up as what it is.
3.sheetLine: The pressure came and the load wasn't taken up.

4.tense: Strength is being spent here under someone else's name — the credit handed off without a glance.
4.verb: bearing what has weight, without turning rigid under it
4.place: on the road toward a goal, where the going is steady and long
4.ask: Take one small step this week toward what you want from this road, with no audience and nobody to credit.
4.core:
You're bearing more on this road than you'll claim — absorbing the setback, carrying the extra mile — and if asked, you'd say it's what anyone would do. The strength being spent belongs to you, and it isn't filed under your name. That's not modesty exactly. It's a grip on your own effort that's gone loose, like you've been carrying somebody else's bag and stopped noticing the strap.

Start where you actually want to go. Take a small step this week toward what you want from this road — plainly, to yourself, no audience, nobody to credit. You might be surprised what's already under the hand once the effort has your name on it.
4.sheetLine: You're carrying more than you'll claim.

1.tense: The weight is here now, and you are still under it.
1.verb: Bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
1.place: Where the body takes the load before anything is decided
1.ask: With someone who is carrying something heavy, stay in touch through the hard part this week. Don't fix it, don't lift it, don't take it onto yourself. And let your own weight rest on your own feet while you do.
1.core:
The weight is here, and it hasn't flattened you. You can bear what has to be borne and hold it without squeezing — the tiredness moves through and you keep your shape, and the pressure doesn't turn you hard at the edges. That isn't rigidity. It's a body that can take load and stay soft, and it's doing that right now, whether or not anyone notices.

Someone close to you is carrying something this week. Sit with them in it instead of fixing it — don't lift it, don't hand them a solution, don't put it on your own shoulders — and let your own two feet hold your own weight while you're there. Staying through the hard part, once, on purpose, with one person, is what shows you what's already yours.
1.sheetLine: You can hold what's heavy and still stay soft at the edges.

2.tense: You are bracing already for a weight that hasn't arrived yet.
2.verb: Bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
2.place: Where the body takes the load before anything is decided
2.ask: When help or thanks comes your way, take it without matching it right away. Let one turn run one way and the next run the other, and keep no tally.
2.core:
You're bracing for something that hasn't arrived. Where holding is needed, the grip has tightened past what the moment asks — the same strength that used to carry the load now spends itself on the next one, and what was steady has started to feel like holding on. From inside, it feels like being ready. From the other side of the door, it looks like nothing can get in.

Letting an exchange move both ways is the way back. When something is offered — help, thanks, someone taking a turn — take it and don't match it straight away. Let one exchange go one way and the next go the other, and keep no count of either. You're not out of proportion; you've overcorrected, and one unmeasured turn puts the measure back.
2.sheetLine: The grip has tightened past what the moment is asking.

3.tense: The pressure came, and you were somewhere else when it landed.
3.verb: Bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
3.place: Where the body takes the load before anything is decided
3.ask: Pick something you've been carrying that no longer needs carrying, set it down on purpose, and let your hands be still a while. Not by dropping it — by laying it down and leaving it there.
3.core:
The pressure came, and something in you went elsewhere. Where weight has to be borne, bearing it stopped being something you do and became something that reads as already done to you. What you can carry is still yours. It just went quiet, and nothing new is getting through while you wait at a threshold that's already behind you.

What comes back through is release, not more effort. Choose something you've been carrying that doesn't need carrying anymore, lay it down deliberately, and let your hands be still for a while. Not dropping it — setting it down with your own hands and walking away from it. Hands remember how to be empty faster than thinking does, and that's what brings you back to the pressure you're actually under.
3.sheetLine: Hands remember empty, and that's the way back.

4.tense: You carry the weight and don't count it as anything you did.
4.verb: Bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
4.place: Where the body takes the load before anything is decided
4.ask: Think of what you actually want, not what would help someone and not what is owed. Take a small step toward it, and tell nobody. The step is the whole of it.
4.core:
The bearing is happening, and you wouldn't call it bearing. You take the weight when it comes and you hand the credit to the day, to the circumstances, to anyone but you — the strength in the scene is treated as the scene's, not yours. What you can hold is not a stranger's gift. It's yours, and it has been doing its work while you looked elsewhere for the author of it.

Wanting is the way back to seeing it. Choose something you actually want, not something that would help someone and not something owed, and take a small step toward it. Tell nobody about the step. It's yours in a way the bearing has felt like it belonged to circumstances, and one plainly yours move is how the strength becomes something you can name.
4.sheetLine: The strength you don't count is still yours, still holding.

1.tense: You are bearing the weight right now without breaking and without bracing.
1.verb: Enduring what presses down and keeping your shape
1.place: In a practice you keep at alone, through repetition
1.ask: Next time someone you love is in it, sit with them a while. Take in what they're carrying. Stay yourself while you do. No fixing, no merging — two people, one hard thing.
1.core:
You can take weight. Put something heavy on you and you hold it, without hardening and without leaning in so far you disappear. Years of repeated work have left you with more room in you than most people have. People feel it. They bring you the hard stuff because you don't flinch and you don't take over.

But holding isn't the same as going still. The other half is staying in contact while you bear it. Next time someone leans on you, let yourself be reached by what they're carrying and stay on your own side of it — near, not fused. That isn't softer. It's what lets the two of you keep breathing in the same room.
1.sheetLine: You hold the weight and still let it reach you.

2.tense: Somewhere ahead you are already bracing for weight that has not arrived.
2.verb: Enduring what presses down and keeping your shape
2.place: In a practice you keep at alone, through repetition
2.ask: This week, name what you're braced for and ask what's actually owed there. Give that much. Then stop, before the extra. No paying for a future that hasn't happened.
2.core:
The strength is real. The trouble is you're spending it early. In your practice you tighten before there's anything to tighten against — the rope pulled taut with nothing on the other end. It feels like readiness. From outside it looks like rigidity, and the body pays either way. What you're carrying is getting carried past the point where carrying helps.

So bring something back to size. Name what you're braced for, ask what the moment actually calls for, do exactly that, and set the rest down. Not less effort. The right amount, no more. Where every obligation has turned into a debt to be worked off, give what's fair and quit the arithmetic. Strength that can loosen holds longer.
2.sheetLine: You're gripping past what the moment asks of you.

3.tense: For a while now, when the weight comes down, something in you has slipped out from under it.
3.verb: Enduring what presses down and keeping your shape
3.place: In a practice you keep at alone, through repetition
3.ask: Take a load you're still holding that finished its work already. Set it down on purpose. Not losing it — letting it go. Rest your hands a while and see what the room feels like.
3.core:
Right now, holding feels dangerous, so you don't. When pressure comes, something folds instead of bearing, and the practice that used to steady you has gone thin. That isn't a flaw in you. It's a load that kept being carried with nowhere to set it down, and the bearing part went quiet. The strength has not left. It's stalled, waiting on something to be put down before it can stand again.

That's the way back: let go on purpose. Find a responsibility, a half-finished effort, an outcome you keep checking — something done, or something that was yours only by habit — and set it down. Not because you failed. Because it's finished. Rest your hands and notice you're still on your feet. The bearing comes back once there's room for it.
3.sheetLine: You folded because there was nowhere to set it down.

4.tense: This strength keeps running, and you have not once counted yourself as its owner.
4.verb: Enduring what presses down and keeping your shape
4.place: In a practice you keep at alone, through repetition
4.ask: Think back to what first pulled you into this practice — the reason, before it became routine. Go face that again this week. Know plainly what you want there. Privately. Nobody else has to hear it.
4.core:
You carry more than you credit yourself with. The steady work, the showing up, the strength that keeps things standing — you'd call it just what you do. Anyone standing next to you calls it that, if not the whole structure. Same when something drops you: you don't see how much you were under, or that going down was honest.

So go back to the reason. There's a person, a craft, a want — whatever it was that pulled you into this before it turned into repetition. Face it again this week and let yourself want it plainly, in private. That original pull is what all this runs on. Remembering it puts your hand back where it has been the whole time.
4.sheetLine: The strength is yours. You just haven't signed for it.

1.tense: You are holding what is yours to carry, and nothing is getting bent under the weight.
1.verb: holding what is yours to carry
1.place: at the doorway between what is out there and what is coming in
1.ask: Next time someone close to you is struggling, don't steady them. Let a little of what they're carrying reach you and stay a while, and notice where you stop and they start.
1.core:
Something is arriving and your body is set up to receive it. Not because you braced for it — because you can stand there while it crosses the threshold, and you don't have to squeeze it down to a size you control. When something hard shows up, it doesn't have to be crushed, and you don't have to be crushed either. That is what holding is supposed to feel like.

You can receive it, hand it on, and keep your own side. Next time someone near you is struggling, let some of what they carry reach you — don't jump in to fix it, and don't put it down for them. Just stay while it's there. You'll feel the edge between you and them stay in place.
1.sheetLine: You can take the weight without going rigid or folding.

2.tense: You are bracing for something that hasn't arrived yet, and the bracing is heavier than whatever is coming.
2.verb: holding what is yours to carry
2.place: at the doorway between what is out there and what is coming in
2.ask: Think of something you're guarding against that isn't here. Let the guard down for it — stop standing behind that door — and see whether your strength was ever the door.
2.core:
Something is on its way in, and your body has already answered, ahead of it. Every unknown gets a wall thrown up, and the walls are heavier than the day. That isn't the same as hardening yourself. This is the part of you that can bear a great deal, posted at a door that doesn't exist yet, holding a weight that hasn't landed.

Try this instead of the strain: take whatever you are guarding against that hasn't arrived and stand down from it — one door you don't watch. The strength stays. It just doesn't have a job that makes the day heavy.
2.sheetLine: You're carrying tomorrow's weight on today's shoulders.

3.tense: You once held something that came in, and since then nothing has crossed the threshold.
3.verb: holding what is yours to carry
3.place: at the doorway between what is out there and what is coming in
3.ask: Find something you're still carrying only because it's still there. Set it down deliberately this week, not dropped, not lost — and stand a while with your hands free.
3.core:
Something came in and it was too much, and the part that holds went quiet. So now the door stands and nothing crosses it. You don't brace against what's coming; you don't expect to meet it at all. You can see the door from here, and it's behind you. What isn't here is the belief that meeting it on the other side would go better than last time.

Waiting on the other side of that door isn't more weight. It's the part of you that was going to be able to hold it. Pick up something you are still carrying from before and put it down deliberately — not lose it, not drop it, set it down — then stand with your hands free and see that you're still upright.
3.sheetLine: It was too much once, so you've stopped standing at the door.

4.tense: You did the work of holding while a story in your head said it was someone else doing it.
4.verb: holding what is yours to carry
4.place: at the doorway between what is out there and what is coming in
4.ask: Recall the last time something pulled you in without you having to talk yourself into it. Turn toward it once this week and notice your own feet doing the moving.
4.core:
Something is arriving that already has your name on it, and you've been treating it as someone else's achievement. Not modesty — a reaching toward a picture of yourself you can't find nearby, while what's actually around you is full of things you built. The strength holding the door is yours. Somehow you'd tell it as just keeping things steady.

What pulled you here to begin with is still there. Bring back the thing that drew you — a craft, a person, a place — and turn toward it once this week, no plan attached. Watch your own feet move. This is yours, and the sooner you see it the less of it you'll spend doubting.
4.sheetLine: You've been holding the place up and calling it someone else.

1.tense: You are holding what needs holding right now, and it has not gone rigid in your hands.
1.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
1.place: where the scales are set level again
1.ask: When someone close brings you something heavy, sit with it beside them for a minute, then say plainly where you stand. Both can be true at once.
1.core:
You can take weight without going stiff, and in the places where fairness gets settled between two people, that steadiness does real work. Nothing here is clenched. You lift what needs lifting, you stay recognisable, and what you carry doesn't decide your shape.

What feeds this is contact that leaves both people whole. So when someone near you is under something, stand beside them rather than above or inside. Let what they are feeling reach you without making it yours to fix, then keep your own footing and say plainly what is yours. Both sides real at once, neither swallowed. You hold only what you agreed to hold, and you stay someone while you do it.
1.sheetLine: You hold it steady, and you don't vanish into it.

2.tense: You are bracing for a weight that hasn't landed yet, and the bracing has started to feel like the work.
2.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
2.place: where the scales are set level again
2.ask: Look at what you're holding for other people and rebalance one share. Hand back what belongs to them, then stop there — no lesson, no debt, nothing to collect.
2.core:
The grip has outrun the need. You pick things up before they ask to be picked up, and hold them tighter than the situation calls for. From outside it reads as strength. From inside it is a fist kept closed against a future you cannot see arriving.

Fairness is the way back, and it stays small. Somewhere in your arms there is a portion that belongs to someone else. Set it back where it came from, without dressing it up as a lesson or a penalty. No ledger to keep. Just the load returned to its owner, and then you stop adjusting. An arm that was locked becomes an arm that moves.
2.sheetLine: You're holding weight that isn't yours because you got there first.

3.tense: You stood at that door a long time ago, and you are still standing in the same spot.
3.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
3.place: where the scales are set level again
3.ask: Choose something you've been carrying since bearing things stopped feeling safe, and set it down this week by deciding to. Leave your hands free of it and notice what's there.
3.core:
Bearing gave out, and something in you decided the bearing itself was the dangerous part. So you stopped lifting, and where the strength used to sit there is an open, unguarded place. You are still at that door. Nothing you picked up back there has been set down deliberately; it still waits in your arms.

Letting go does what effort can't. Take one load that belongs to then rather than to your life now, and release it on purpose — deciding, not losing. Your hands stay free of it for a while. Nobody asks you to pick up anything new. Strength comes back by itself to a body no longer guarding a door it already walked through.
3.sheetLine: You're still holding a door that closed behind you.

4.tense: You are holding things level without noticing the hand that keeps them upright.
4.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
4.place: where the scales are set level again
4.ask: Recall a moment you acted because you wanted to, not because it was owed, and tell yourself you chose it. Then move a little toward that again.
4.core:
There is strength in you that you keep setting down as though it belonged to the room. People are steadier because you were there, and you would call that the situation being fine by itself. The hand keeping things level belongs to you, and you don't count it.

What brought you here was wanting something and moving toward it before you knew it would work. That pull is still in you, unattended. So look back at a moment you acted for no reason but wanting, and say plainly that you chose it. Then take a small step toward something the same shape this week, for nobody's benefit but your own. Light lands on what was cultivated first, and you have been cultivating without looking.
4.sheetLine: The hand keeping things level is your own.

1.tense: The hand has already decided, and it is still holding the pen.
1.verb: bearing what has to be borne until the bearing is done
1.place: at the point where the grip is let go
1.ask: Someone near you is carrying something heavy. Sit with them without fixing it. Let what they hold land on you a little, and keep your own footing while it does.
1.core:
You can stand under something heavy without stiffening around it. That is not passivity — the load gets carried and the body stays open. Where you tend what matters, you put weight in and then let the result land where it lands. People feel they can lean in without getting squeezed.

But strength can go lonely when nothing is allowed to reach it. Someone near you is being managed rather than felt, and you keep just enough distance to stay steady. Let their load touch you this week and stay on your own feet anyway. A hand on your arm you do not shrug off, a story you do not redirect, a silence you let stay sad. You do not have to carry them. You just have to stop going numb in order to stay strong.
1.sheetLine: You can keep your footing and still be moved by what they carry.

2.tense: The bracing is already happening for a week that has not arrived.
2.verb: bearing what has to be borne until the bearing is done
2.place: at the point where the grip is let go
2.ask: Look at what you are holding for other people. Give back what was not yours to carry, keep what is, then stop there. No tally of who owes what.
2.core:
Endurance in the right amount is a floor. Too much and it turns to a vise — what is yours and what is not both end up gripped, and the grip starts to feel like the point. You brace for the next thing before the last one has finished, and people feel it. Steadiness starts reading as control, and it costs you the closeness you were trying to keep.

Proportion is the way back. Look honestly at what is in your hands — is all of this actually mine, and how much does it need today? Hold that much, then stop. Fairness here is not punishment; it is just the right size. One day at the correct weight teaches you what your arms have been doing. What belonged to someone else can go back to them without anyone being blamed.
2.sheetLine: You are gripping harder than the thing requires.

3.tense: The door closed, and the body is still standing in the doorway.
3.verb: bearing what has to be borne until the bearing is done
3.place: at the point where the grip is let go
3.ask: Something in your life is over, and part of you keeps tending it anyway — a message, a worry, a role you keep answering. Stop feeding that one for a while.
3.core:
When the weight came, the strength went quiet. Holding anything after that felt like the very thing that had failed, and the hands learned to let go early, before a grip could form. That kept you moving. It also means things pass through without being carried, and you may notice you are not where you intended to be. A door behind you is still taking your weight.

Releasing on purpose is different from losing your grip. One thing has already ended and something in you refills it anyway. Stop feeding that one thing and watch where your weight goes instead. Empty hands are allowed to stay empty. That is not defeat, and it is not the pause before some next noble carry. It is just empty, and that is allowed.
3.sheetLine: You let go before you got to hold it.

4.tense: The hand is doing the work, and the name on it has gone missing.
4.verb: bearing what has to be borne until the bearing is done
4.place: at the point where the grip is let go
4.ask: Out of everything you are holding, pick the one that matters most to you, and turn toward it this week. Whatever has been pulling at you can wait its turn.
4.core:
You are bearing a lot, and none of it feels authored by you. When it holds, you credit the timing or the people around. When it gives way, you take the whole blame. Either way you are watching rather than doing — the strength and the collapse running without your hand in them. Nobody asked what you wanted, so the asking stopped.

Wanting is not selfish, and it does not have to become a plan. Out of everything you are carrying, choose the one that matters most, and turn toward it this week. No chasing, no announcing. Let it be wanted, to yourself, and see how the weight feels once it has a direction pointing somewhere you picked. You were already steering by something. This just lets you face it on purpose.
4.sheetLine: You already chose the direction. You just don't count it as yours.

1.tense: The bearing is happening right now, and the pen is here with it.
1.verb: bearing what must be borne without breaking or going rigid
1.place: at a threshold where something is ending so something else can start
1.ask: Spend ten minutes with someone who is in the middle of something hard — no fixing, no advice — while you stay on your own feet.
1.core:
You can carry a heavy thing and stay soft with it. That is the strength that doesn't need to squeeze to know its own shape. People lean on you because you don't creak under them, and you don't crush them either.

Where something is ending in your life, this is the hour it is asking for. Not the ending you force, and not the one you refuse — the one you let land. Reach for the people who are in it with you. Sit beside one of them in what they are carrying without lifting it off them. That is what your strength is for now.
1.sheetLine: You can hold what's heavy without gripping it.

2.tense: A future nobody can write in advance is the one this strength is bracing against.
2.verb: bearing what must be borne without breaking or going rigid
2.place: at a threshold where something is ending so something else can start
2.ask: Take one uneven load between you and someone and settle the share — hand part back, claim your part — then leave it alone.
2.core:
Under pressure you hold on tighter, and the tightness takes over the job the ending was supposed to do. A thing that is over, you're still propping up with your shoulder. What was resilience has turned into a grip, and the grip has taken the whole seat.

What is needed here is fairer than more bearing. Some of what sits on you belongs to somebody else, and setting it down isn't dropping it — it's putting the load back where it came from. Settle one share this week: hand back a piece that isn't yours, or take back the piece that is. Then stop. The floor holds without you propping it, and the people leaning might prefer the room. You could find out.
2.sheetLine: You're propping up something that's already finished.

3.tense: A door behind you is closed, and you are still standing at it, waiting.
3.verb: bearing what must be borne without breaking or going rigid
3.place: at a threshold where something is ending so something else can start
3.ask: Set down something you've been gripping past its finish, and go a day with your palms open before you pick up the next thing.
3.core:
When the weight came, the bearing went quiet. You reach for the quick answer now, and the quick answer is what lands, and the steadier one has stopped being offered. Holding anything feels like it might break you, so you hold nothing, and the nothing has its own heaviness. Going well, this would be a flat, level floor that carries what is set on it and lets it be set down again, with no one the worse for either.

Strength isn't the missing piece. Setting down what you've been gripping past its ending is. Let one thing go on purpose — not by losing it, by releasing it — and walk a day with your hands free. What they hold after will be lighter, and yours.
3.sheetLine: You keep waiting at a door that already closed.

4.tense: The pen is down in a room you are already writing in, and you haven't noticed the page.
4.verb: bearing what must be borne without breaking or going rigid
4.place: at a threshold where something is ending so something else can start
4.ask: Name the thing you'd hate most to lose, and give it an hour — one step, quiet, no plan past that. Wanting it is allowed.
4.core:
You have been holding things up for a while, and it reads to you as ordinary. What people lean on is not a mood you happen to be in; it is a strength you keep using while telling yourself you're not. The same goes for the times you fell apart. Both get filed by you as passing conditions.

What is actually yours here is a direction. Something drew you before any of this got heavy, and you can still name it if you stop long enough. Pick the thing you'd hate most to lose, and give it an hour this week — one step, no announcement. You knew which one it was before you finished asking. Let that count as knowing.
4.sheetLine: You've been carrying it without counting yourself the carrier.

1.tense: You are carrying what has to be carried right now, in a way that can flex.
1.verb: bearing what's in front of you without going rigid
1.place: at the point where you keep adjusting, moment to moment
1.ask: Next time someone close to you is struggling, sit with them a few minutes and don't fix it — no advice, no tidying. Keep your own sense of things while you do.
1.core:
There's a weight on you at the moment and you're carrying it without hardening around it. When something hurts and you stay soft enough to keep adjusting, that isn't weakness leaking through — that's the thing working. You can feel where the pressure is and you're not pretending it away.

So let some of it be shared. Next time someone close to you is struggling, sit with them a few minutes and don't fix it — no advice, no tidying them up. Keep your own sense of things while you do. You'll find you can hold their weight and yours at once without either going flat, and that nobody has to be absorbed into the other for it to count.
1.sheetLine: You can carry this and still bend.

2.tense: You are bracing against what might come next, holding harder than the moment requires.
2.verb: bearing what's in front of you without going rigid
2.place: at the point where you keep adjusting, moment to moment
2.ask: Where a load is carried alongside someone else, shift the share until it's genuinely even, then stop — say out loud you've stopped, and leave their half with them.
2.core:
You're holding things so far ahead that your grip has stopped being about now. What used to bend has stiffened into something braced. You're set for a strain that hasn't arrived, and that bracing is costing you the ease you'd need to meet the one that does. Around you, people feel the over-tightness without being able to name it.

What's thin here isn't effort, it's proportion. Where a load is carried alongside someone else, shift the share until it's genuinely even, then stop — say out loud you've stopped, and leave their half with them. You don't have to keep compensating in advance; you can find the fair point, put it down, and the ground under you is steadier for it, not less.
2.sheetLine: You're holding so hard the shape has stopped being true.

3.tense: Under pressure you folded, and you have not come back out to where the pressure is.
3.verb: bearing what's in front of you without going rigid
3.place: at the point where you keep adjusting, moment to moment
3.ask: Choose something you've been clutching and set it down for a few days — not lost, just placed where you can see it. Wait with your hands free and notice what's there.
3.core:
There was a load you couldn't carry, and something in you learned that holding is where it breaks. Since then you've stayed clear of the places where weight gets put on you, and from the outside it looks like calm. Inside, you're stationed at a door you've already walked through, checking whether it's safe to come back.

Setting something down is what brings you back. Choose something you've been clutching and set it down for a few days — not lost, just placed where you can see it. Wait with your hands free and notice what's there. You'll find that letting go on your own terms doesn't feel like the floor giving way, and the next weight arrives at a strength that was already yours.
3.sheetLine: You're guarding a threshold you already crossed.

4.tense: You are bearing what you bear without seeing that the strength is yours.
4.verb: bearing what's in front of you without going rigid
4.place: at the point where you keep adjusting, moment to moment
4.ask: Name something you'd like, small and only yours, and take one step toward it this week — before calling it sensible. Then notice who moved.
4.core:
There's strength in how you hold things, and also a version where you keep collapsing under what others seem to manage — and you don't count yourself as either. The hands doing the work don't get named. You talk about getting through as if it happened to you rather than being the way you operate.

Wanting is the way back in. Name something you'd like, small and only yours, and take one step toward it this week — before calling it sensible, before checking it against anyone's needs. Then notice who moved. You'll find the desire and the loading come from the same place, and that seeing where you're going tells you whose strength has been under it the whole time.
4.sheetLine: The strength in your hands is yours and goes unnamed.

1.tense: Right now you are carrying something, and it is not changing your shape.
1.verb: bearing what is laid on you without either breaking or turning to stone
1.place: the bare shape of a thing, with the particular weight lifted off it
1.ask: When someone hands you the weight of their day, sit with it beside them and feel what it costs you while you listen. Stay with them and stay your own — not fused, not gone.
1.core:
There is something on you and it is not bending you. That is the plain version of what is working: the weight is real, your outline is intact, and you are not white-knuckling to keep it that way. When you look at a hard thing and see its workings — where the pressure comes from, what would happen if it were set down — you bear it better than you did when you were only bracing. Seeing the shape of a load is not the same as taking it on. You can do the first without the second.

The next thing this can feed is other people. Not fixing them and not holding them up. Sitting with someone who is under something, letting their weight register on you while you keep your own side, is a small act with a clear edge. It keeps the work honest, because strength that only ever runs alone starts to think it is the only one in the building.
1.sheetLine: You can hold this without losing your shape.

2.tense: You will be braced for a pressure that has not arrived and may never arrive.
2.verb: bearing what is laid on you without either breaking or turning to stone
2.place: the bare shape of a thing, with the particular weight lifted off it
2.ask: When you catch yourself braced for something that is not here, look at what is actually on you today and bring the grip down to meet it. No more than that, and then stop.
2.core:
Something in you is getting ready early. You are gripping before there is anything to grip, checking the strap before the strap has a job — and the bracing itself now costs what the weight would have. From inside it feels like strength. From outside the muscle is simply locked. What you are guarding is not in danger yet, and staying clenched until it is means you arrive at the real thing already worn down. The pattern you see so clearly — how it will go, what will be asked — is a forecast, not a fact. You read mechanism better than most, which is exactly why the forecast feels solid.

A way back is smaller than it sounds. Fairness here is not punishment and not reward. It is the grip matching the load.
2.sheetLine: You're bracing for weight that hasn't landed yet.

3.tense: Something came down on you and you have been standing at that door ever since.
3.verb: bearing what is laid on you without either breaking or turning to stone
3.place: the bare shape of a thing, with the particular weight lifted off it
3.ask: Take what you have been holding since then — a version of events, a duty, a grudge — and release it on purpose. Sit with empty hands a while and notice what they do.
3.core:
Something landed and you went down under it, and you have been braced for the next one since. That is why holding now looks like standing near an exit. From where you are standing the door is still open and something is still coming. It is not. You are clear about how pressure works — you can see the mechanism, the shape of a load, the way a thing gives — and that clarity has turned into a reason not to pick anything up at all. Knowing how a thing collapses is not the same as knowing it will. The strength you cannot locate has not gone anywhere; it is set down while you watch the door.

Put down the grip, not the load. There is a specific thing you have been holding past the point it needed holding, and letting go of it once is small enough to try today.
3.sheetLine: Holding anything feels dangerous since then.

4.tense: You are already doing the thing you say you cannot do.
4.verb: bearing what is laid on you without either breaking or turning to stone
4.place: the bare shape of a thing, with the particular weight lifted off it
4.ask: Think of the last thing you were drawn toward before you decided it wasn't for you, and give it honest attention again — not to act on it, just to look at what pulled you.
4.core:
There is strength in this account and a collapse in this account, and neither is filed under your name. You would say you are just getting through. Meanwhile you are the person holding the shape while others come apart in it, and the person who goes flat for a week and calls it tired. Both are you. The pattern is right there and you keep reading it as conditions. What you see so clearly in how things work, you do not turn on yourself — your own case gets described from the outside. That is not modesty. It is a blind spot with good manners.

What you want is a better clue than what you are enduring. There was something you were drawn to before you ruled it out. Face it again — not to act on it, just to look plainly. The pull is yours, and nobody made it for you.
4.sheetLine: You hold more than you give yourself credit for.

1.tense: Right now, in what you're carrying, you can hold weight without going rigid, and the floor stays steady under you.
1.verb: bearing weight without breaking
1.place: at the sudden clearing, where the false structure falls away
1.ask: Something in your care is wobbling this week. Stay near it — or near whoever is holding it — without stepping back and without taking it over. Keep showing up while it's unsteady.
1.core:
Right now, you can hold what has to be held and stay soft in it at once. You don't grip to make the load lighter, and you don't let go to make it easier on yourself. People stand on that floor without ever being told it's there. That's the whole of what you do with it.

Something in your care is about to come down — maybe a structure you built, maybe one you only leaned on. When it falls, don't brace and don't rush to pick it back up. Sit with whoever is in it. You might think staying near means fixing. It doesn't. You can feel the weight alongside someone and keep your own feet under your own chair. That is the practice. What you cannot hold, you don't have to carry for them.
1.sheetLine: You can hold the weight and stay soft doing it.

2.tense: You're bracing for something that hasn't happened yet, holding it so hard the holding itself is becoming the load.
2.verb: bearing weight without breaking
2.place: at the sudden clearing, where the false structure falls away
2.ask: Look at the load you're carrying that isn't yours alone. Adjust the share — give back the part that belongs to someone else, keep what's yours — and once it's fair, stop.
2.core:
Something in your care may come down, and you've decided to keep it up by strength alone. Your grip is doing what a brace does — it holds, and it can't let anything move. What was steady in you is getting stiff, and the stiffness reads as strength. It's the arm holding the wall so the wall doesn't have to hold itself.

Not every structure deserves the weight of your whole body, and your arm isn't what keeps anyone honest. Shift what you are carrying until the load is fairly split, then stop shifting. Some people will mind that you stopped reaching first. A few will ask why the posture changed. Tell them what's actually true about it, plainly, and leave the answer with them.
2.sheetLine: You're keeping something up that wants to come down.

3.tense: There was pressure, and you let go of what you were holding, and nothing in you has reached for anything solid since.
3.verb: bearing weight without breaking
3.place: at the sudden clearing, where the false structure falls away
3.ask: Notice what you're still half-carrying that you already decided to stop carrying. Set that down — not everything, just the one that's already finished. Nothing gets concluded by setting it down.
3.core:
When the weight came, holding it felt like more than you could do, so you stopped holding. What used to be yours to carry, you now set down before it starts. The door behind you already closed. You're still in front of it. Nothing about that says anything about what you're made of.

You don't need to pick up the whole thing again. That isn't what this is asking. There is something you have already decided to stop carrying, and your hands haven't gotten the message yet. Put that down. Nothing has to be concluded by setting it down. If it turns out you want it back, you can pick it up. Your hands will have told you something in the meantime.
3.sheetLine: You put things down before they get heavy.

4.tense: You're holding something steady right now, and if someone said so you'd credit luck, or the situation, or anyone but your own grip.
4.verb: bearing weight without breaking
4.place: at the sudden clearing, where the false structure falls away
4.ask: Take one small step this week toward something you'd want a year from now. No plan, no announcement to anyone. Just the one step, and nothing has to be committed by taking it.
4.core:
You're holding something steady right now, and you don't count it. The steady thing might be a job, a routine, a person you keep showing up for. From the outside, it looks like backbone. From the inside, it doesn't register as anything you're doing. When you come apart, the same holds — it gets filed under circumstances.

Go to wanting, before the load. At some point something pulled you toward a version of your life, and you turned without naming it a decision. Take one small step this week toward something you'd want a year from now. No plan and no announcement. The step is small enough that nothing has to be committed by taking it. If it goes nowhere, you'll have learned that. If it goes somewhere, you'll have found the thing your strength is for.
4.sheetLine: The steady thing is you, not the luck.

1.tense: You are here, taking what is heavy, and it is not bending you out of shape.
1.verb: Bearing what's heavy without letting it twist you
1.place: Where you steer by what you actually want
1.ask: Next time someone near you is in something hard, sit in it beside them and fix nothing — keep your own footing the whole way through.
1.core:
You can take weight and not go rigid under it. That's the trick, and it's mostly yours already: what's heavy gets taken, and you stay someone who can set it down when the day is done. Where you're pointed matters. You steer by what you actually want, not by whatever is loudest, and that's why the load doesn't bend you.

The strain shows up in contact. Taking things well can turn into taking them alone, and alone is where strong starts to harden. So the next good move is small. When someone near you is in something hard, sit in it with them and fix nothing. Stay close while it's difficult. Keep your own footing the whole way through — that's the point. You can be near what they're carrying without lifting it off them, and what's already yours stays yours to set down.
1.sheetLine: You take what's heavy without going hard.

2.tense: You will be braced for something that hasn't happened yet, and doing it on purpose.
2.verb: Bearing what's heavy without letting it twist you
2.place: Where you steer by what you actually want
2.ask: Look at one place where you're carrying more than your share. Set it right — one conversation, one clear change — then stop and touch it no further.
2.core:
The strength that carries you is starting to grip. Somewhere ahead is a weight nobody has handed you yet, and you're already braced for it, gripped past what the moment calls for until the grip goes stiff. It looks like strength, and it works like a cage — mostly for the people standing near you.

Fairness is the fix, and it's something you can already do. Look at one place where you're carrying more than is yours and adjust the share until it's even, then stop. Not punishment, not a speech — a correction, then hands off. What it costs is this: you give up being the one who carries all of it. Do it once, plainly, and afterward let each side find its own level. The weight you brace against in advance is usually heavier than the weight itself.
2.sheetLine: You're bracing for weight that hasn't landed yet.

3.tense: Something got heavy, and you set it down before it could land on you.
3.verb: Bearing what's heavy without letting it twist you
3.place: Where you steer by what you actually want
